Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Redirection: I think of something else, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Vignette:
Elena Martinez had spent thirty years as a detective, most of them in the narcotics division of a large city police department. She was known for her steady hands and her ability to read a crime scene like a familiar book. But that ended on a humid Tuesday afternoon in a condemned warehouse on the south side. She had been called to a suspected meth lab; the air inside was thick with a sweet, acrid smell she did not recognize. Within minutes, her throat tightened, her chest burned, and she could not get enough air. She stumbled outside, gasping, while her partner called for an ambulance. In the emergency room, the doctors said it was a combination of solvents and precursor chemicals—likely a concentrated exposure from a hidden tank. She spent three days in the hospital, her lungs raw, her skin stinging from decontamination showers that smelled of antiseptic and bleach.

At first, Elena told herself it was just a bad day. She went back to work after two weeks of sick leave, but her body did not seem to agree. Walking into the precinct, she caught a whiff of bleach from the janitor’s cart and her stomach lurched. She started taking the stairs instead of the elevator because the small, closed space made her feel like she could not breathe. Then came the smells that came from nowhere—the metallic tang of a colleague’s sweat after a foot chase, the faint hospital odor from a first-aid kit—and her hands would fly to her face, covering her nose and mouth as if she could block the world out. She learned to redirect her thoughts when it happened, forcing herself to think of something neutral, like the layout of her own apartment or the names of streets. But the effort exhausted her.

The worst part was the way the memory refused to stay still. When she tried to recall that afternoon, she got only pieces: the yellow light through a grimy window, the sound of her own ragged breathing, a sharp chemical taste that made her gag. The pieces did not connect. She would start to follow them into the moment when she knew she was in danger, and then her mind would simply shut the door. But sometimes, without warning, the whole scene would snap back as if it were happening again—her chest heaving, the room spinning—and she would be back on the warehouse floor, not in her present kitchen or her car. It felt real. It felt now.

Elena had always been a vigilant person; it came with the job. But now her vigilance had no off switch. Every unexpected sound—a car backfiring, a door slamming, a colleague dropping a file folder—sent a jolt through her body. She scanned rooms constantly, looking for exits, for people who moved too quickly. Her shoulders stayed up near her ears. She came to believe that she could not let her guard down, not even for a second, because the moment she did, something would happen again. And somewhere underneath that was a deeper fear: that she had lost the ability to feel like her old self. She worried that she would never laugh the way she used to, never feel anything normal again. Emotions felt distant, behind glass.

The hardest consequence was how she began to shrink her world. Elena stopped going to the precinct social events. She avoided her sergeant, then the captain, then any officer in a uniform that reminded her of the hospital staff who had treated her with brisk efficiency but never really explained what had happened or why no one had warned her about the chemicals before she entered the building. She had trusted the department to keep her safe, and they had not. That sense of institutional failure settled into her bones. She stopped volunteering for cases that required her to enter known hazardous sites. Eventually, she requested a desk reassignment, telling her lieutenant it was for a medical reason. He approved it without asking questions, which only confirmed her feeling that no one really cared.

Alone in her apartment most evenings—her divorce had happened years before the exposure, so there was no one to come home to—Elena found herself jumping at the hum of the refrigerator or the thud of a neighbor’s footsteps. She slept badly, her body braced. What finally drove her to a therapist’s office was a moment at the grocery store: she was reaching for a carton of milk when a child nearby coughed, and the sound triggered such a violent shortness of breath that she dropped to her knees in the aisle, covering her face, gasping for air. A store employee asked if she needed an ambulance. The word itself—ambulance—sent her scrambling out the door without buying anything. That night, sitting on her couch with her hands on her knees, she realized she could not go on like this. She called a psychological services number her union had sent her months ago. She was afraid of what she would find in her own head, but she was more afraid of spending the rest of her life hiding from a smell.
